summary:
Nova Scotia stands under the Canadian national framework, which the parent record carries. Within provincial competence, the province operates no restrictive trans-specific legislation and instead maintains an explicit inclusion framework.

The Government of Nova Scotia released the province's first 2SLGBTQIA+ Action Plan on 8 January 2026, developed under the Dismantling Racism and Hate Act passed in 2022, described by the province as the first Canadian law of its kind to explicitly acknowledge 2SLGBTQIA+ people. The plan was informed by more than 600 community members through surveys, virtual meetings and consultations, and maps actions to improve programs and policies supporting full inclusion of 2SLGBTQIA+ people.

On 10 June 2026 the province announced more than $176,000 through the first round of its 2SLGBTQIA+ Community Impact Grant program, including $25,000 to Pictou County Pride, $25,000 to LakeCity Works' Queer Careers program in Dartmouth, $12,067 to SeaHorse Sexual Health Centre for queer and trans outreach on the Eastern Shore, and $50,000 to Truro Pride to host the province's first provincial 2SLGBTQIA+ conference; per-project grants are capped at $25,000 from the 2025-26 fiscal year.

The documented Nova Scotia case on trans correctional placement concerns a transgender woman from the Halifax region serving a two-year robbery sentence. The Chronicle Herald reported on 18 March 2025 that a federal judge granted her more time to file her application for judicial review of the decision to hold her in a men's prison, citing a lack of transparency and clear, timely communication in the institutional decision-making, and systemic barriers that restricted her access to her lawyer. No later documented instance of this case appears in the record.

Statistics Canada reported on 30 March 2026 that police recorded 4,882 hate crimes nationally in 2024, 1% above 2023, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000, down 2% in 2024 and up 142% since 2018; eight provinces recorded stable or declining rates. The release carries no Nova Scotia-specific rate or incident count. The underlying analysis of sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations comes from Egale Canada, an LGBTIQ+ organisation's report on national police-reported data.

In the 2024 Spartacus Gay Travel Index, Canada including Nova Scotia shared first place with Malta, New Zealand, Spain and Portugal among 213 countries and regions as a travel destination covering lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex people.
tangentialFactors:
Nova Scotia's courts have been part of the national pattern of striking down section 159 of the Criminal Code, which criminalised anal intercourse; the section was declared unconstitutional in Nova Scotia among other provinces and repealed effective 21 June 2019 through Bill C-75, setting the age of consent for anal intercourse at 16.

A 2020 poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office found 87.6% of those surveyed said they would be "comfortable" if a neighbour was a transgender person, against 91.8% for a gay, lesbian or bisexual neighbour. This measures comfort with a neighbour, not law, enforcement or protection outcomes, and the survey window closed years ago.

Other Canadian provinces have moved in a restrictive direction on trans-related school and sport policy, including Saskatchewan's Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act 2023 requiring parental consent for students under 16 requesting use of a gender-related preferred name or gender identity, and Alberta's 2024 Health Statutes Amendment Act, Education Amendment Act and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, which faced legal challenges the Alberta government sought to block through Bill 9 in 2025 using the notwithstanding clause. Nova Scotia has enacted no comparable measure.
localsOnly:
Nova Scotia residents can access the provincial 2SLGBTQIA+ Action Plan and the Community Impact Grant program, which funds local organisations including Pictou County Pride, LakeCity Works' Queer Careers program, SeaHorse Sexual Health Centre and Truro Pride. Grants are capped at $25,000 per project from the 2025-26 fiscal year.

Discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodations is prohibited; as of 2017 all provinces, territories and the federal government explicitly include gender identity as a prohibited ground in their human rights acts. Transgender people can change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules.

The Dismantling Racism and Hate Act, passed in 2022, is described by the province as the first Canadian law of its kind to explicitly acknowledge 2SLGBTQIA+ people and provides the statutory basis for the Action Plan.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Statistics Canada release of 30 March 2026 carries no Nova Scotia-specific hate-crime rate or incident count; the province-level figure is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

The inventory does not document Nova Scotia-specific rules for changing gender markers on provincial documents such as birth certificates or driver's licences; that layer is not sourced in this record.

The inventory does not document Nova Scotia-specific facility-access, healthcare access or school-policy rules for trans residents; no such claim can be verified from these sources.

The trans correctional-placement case is documented only through the 18 March 2025 Chronicle Herald report; its subsequent outcome is not sourced here and remains unresolved.
